uncited: Temporal Input Conditioning parameterizes scene attributes—such as position, rotation, opacity, density, or color—as explicit functions of time $t$ to enable novel view synthesis for dynamic scenes.

It addresses the challenge of modeling non-rigid motion and temporal evolution from monocular or sparse multi-view inputs without requiring ground-truth geometry or dense multi-view stereo data at every instant.

It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into static canonical geometry and time-varying deformation fields, or by conditioning radiance fields directly on time, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture.

Unlike [DaReNeRF](13782-darenerf.md), which focuses on direction-aware wavelet decompositions, this family establishes the foundational canonical-space and time-conditioning paradigms for dynamic neural rendering.
The family builds on the parent's shared principles for handling temporal dynamics [Parent](9265-dynamic-and-temporal-modeling.md).
The concept of temporal input conditioning in neural rendering originated with D-NeRF, which introduced the canonical space paradigm for dynamic scenes.
This approach allows for the decomposition of dynamic scenes into static geometry and time-varying deformations, addressing the limitations of direct 6D mappings.
Subsequent works like DaReNeRF have refined this by introducing direction-aware representations to mitigate artifacts such as shift variance and checkerboard effects.

More recent developments, such as the time-dependent NeRF, integrate these concepts with continuous camera motion optimization, using local temporal neighborhoods to constrain SDF flows and improve pose estimation.
